title: “TELL IT TO THE CHURCH”: THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT MANY CHRISTIANS QUOTE—BUT FEW ARE PREPARED TO OBEY
paragraphs: “TELL IT TO THE CHURCH”: THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT MANY CHRISTIANS QUOTE—BUT FEW ARE PREPARED TO OBEY

When a brother sins, when trust is shattered, and when silence begins to destroy what love was meant to protect, Matthew 18 reveals a difficult truth: Jesus never commanded His Church to cover up sin, weaponize correction, or abandon the wounded. He commanded something far more costly.
There is a kind of pain that only happens inside the Church.
It is not the pain of being rejected by strangers.
It is the pain of being wounded by people who know your prayers.
People who have heard you worship.
People who have called you brother. Sister. Family.
People who have stood beside you with their hands lifted toward heaven, only to leave you wondering how someone who speaks so beautifully about Jesus could treat another human being so cruelly.
And sometimes the wound goes even deeper.
You finally find the courage to speak.
You explain what happened.
You tell someone you trust.
And instead of asking whether you are safe, whether the truth has been established, or whether the wrong can be corrected, someone opens a Bible and says:
“Matthew 18.”
Three words.
And suddenly, the person who was wounded feels as though they are the one standing trial.
But there is another side to this story.
Somewhere, a Christian has sinned against someone they love.
They know what they did.
They have rehearsed excuses in their mind.
They have prayed for the guilt to disappear without ever making things right.
They still attend church. Still sing. Still serve. Still post Scriptures.
But there is a conversation they are avoiding.
An apology they have not offered.
A truth they have not confessed.
And every time Matthew 18 is mentioned, something inside them becomes uncomfortable.
Because deep down, they know.
Jesus is not merely speaking to the wounded.
He is also speaking to the one who caused the wound.

And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that both people can be sitting in the same congregation, listening to the same sermon, while carrying entirely different reasons to fear the words of Christ.
Now listen carefully.
What if the passage that has been used to silence wounded Christians was actually given to protect the holiness of Christ's people?
What if the passage that has been used to justify harsh public humiliation was actually designed to make restoration possible?
And what if the words “tell it to the church” reveal something much deeper than a procedure for resolving disagreements?
Something about the heart of Jesus.
Something about the seriousness of sin.
Something about the danger of pride.
And something about the kind of love that refuses to surrender a soul to destruction.
Because before Jesus ever said, “Tell it to the church,” He told a story about a sheep.
And unless we understand that sheep, we may completely misunderstand the Church.
In Matthew 18:12–14, Jesus describes a shepherd who has one hundred sheep. One wanders away, and the shepherd goes looking for the one that has strayed.
The point is not that the other ninety-nine have become worthless.
The point is that the wandering one has not become disposable.
Then Jesus says:
“Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” — Matthew 18:14, WEB
Read that again.
Before confrontation, there is concern.
Before discipline, there is a shepherd's heart.
Before the difficult conversation, there is a Savior who does not treat wandering souls as worthless.
This is the atmosphere in which Matthew 18:15–20 must be understood.
Not revenge.
Not institutional image management.
Not a competition to prove who is more righteous.
But a holy concern for truth, repentance, protection, and the recovery of a brother or sister whenever restoration is possible.
Then Jesus says something that confronts both our fear of conflict and our appetite for gossip.
“If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” — Matthew 18:15, WEB
The Greek text contains a remarkable expression.
ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου
ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou
“You have gained your brother.”
The verb ἐκέρδησας comes from κερδαίνω (kerdainō), meaning to gain or win.
Jesus does not describe the goal as winning the argument.
He describes it as gaining the brother.
There is a difference.
A devastating difference.
One person confronts because they want someone humiliated.
Another confronts because they want the truth acknowledged, the wrong addressed, and a relationship restored if genuine repentance makes that possible.
One wants to say, “I told you so.”
The other longs to say, “Thank God we did not allow this sin to destroy us.”
That is not weakness.
That is love governed by truth.
But notice something equally important.
Jesus does not say, “Pretend nothing happened.”
He does not say, “Call evil good because you are supposed to forgive.”
He does not say, “Protect the reputation of the person who harmed you at the expense of justice.”
He says to address the wrong.
The Greek verb commonly translated “show him his fault” is ἔλεγξον (elenxon), from ἐλέγχω (elenchō).
It carries the sense of exposing, correcting, or bringing a wrong to light.
Not inventing accusations.
Not assuming guilt without evidence.
Not turning suspicion into certainty.
But bringing a genuine wrong into the light where it can be confronted truthfully.
And that matters because a Church that refuses to confront sin is not necessarily a loving Church.
Sometimes it is simply a frightened Church.
Frightened of uncomfortable conversations.
Frightened of losing influential people.
Frightened of financial consequences.
Frightened of discovering that someone admired has been living dishonestly.
Frightened of what will happen when the truth becomes impossible to ignore.
But Jesus did not die to create a community where appearances matter more than righteousness.
He died to redeem sinners and make a people holy.
There is also a textual detail worth understanding.

Some Greek manuscripts of Matthew 18:15 include the words εἰς σέ (eis se), meaning “against you,” while others omit them. That is why some Bible translations read, “If your brother sins against you,” while others read more broadly, “If your brother sins.”
This variation should not be hidden from readers.
It reminds us to interpret the passage carefully rather than building an entire doctrine upon a disputed phrase.

The immediate context certainly includes personal wrongdoing and relationships within the community of believers. Yet the wider New Testament also teaches that serious sin must be addressed appropriately, even when it is not merely a private offense against one individual.
And here is where many people misunderstand Jesus.
They turn the first step into an absolute rule that every injured person must privately confront every offender before seeking help.
But Matthew 18 was never intended to prohibit victims from seeking protection, reporting crimes, involving responsible authorities, or obtaining necessary support.
If someone is being abused, threatened, coerced, or placed in danger, they do not have to meet privately with the person harming them.
If a child has been harmed, the priority is protection, not arranging a private conversation with the alleged offender.
If there is a credible allegation of criminal conduct, reporting it to the appropriate authorities is not disobedience to Jesus.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining wrongdoing.
Matthew 18 does not cancel that responsibility.
And when allegations concern a church leader, other biblical passages, including 1 Timothy 5:19–20, provide additional guidance about evidence, accountability, and public correction when warranted.
Biblical confrontation is not a weapon for forcing vulnerable people into unsafe situations.
It is a call to deal with sin faithfully.
Jesus never asked His people to confuse secrecy with holiness.
The first private conversation in Matthew 18 serves a meaningful purpose when it is appropriate and safe.
It prevents unnecessary public exposure.
It creates an opportunity for repentance without needless humiliation.
It protects against careless gossip.
It gives someone a chance to acknowledge wrong before an entire community becomes involved.
Imagine how many relationships could be spared unnecessary damage if Christians stopped discussing someone else's failure with ten people before speaking truthfully to the person concerned.
Imagine how many church divisions begin with a conversation that never should have happened.
A whisper after worship.
A screenshot forwarded to a friend.
A prayer request that is actually disguised gossip.
A private disagreement turned into a public campaign.
Someone says, “I am only telling you so you can pray.”
But sometimes what we call a prayer request is simply gossip wearing religious clothing.
And the Lord sees the difference.
Proverbs 16:28 warns that a whisperer separates close friends.
James 1:19 calls believers to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
The Bible does not treat words as harmless.
A reputation can be damaged in minutes.
A friendship can be fractured by half a story.
An entire congregation can become divided because people were more interested in choosing sides than discovering what was true.
And yet, the opposite mistake is just as dangerous.
Some people hear “go privately” and conclude that serious wrongdoing must remain hidden indefinitely.
No.
Privacy is not the same as concealment.
Discretion is not the same as complicity.
And forgiveness is not the same as pretending a person is safe when their behavior demonstrates otherwise.
If the person listens, Jesus says, you have gained your brother.
But what if they do not listen?
What if they deny what is established?
What if they refuse to acknowledge the wrong?
What if they continue causing harm?
Jesus continues:
“But if he doesn't listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.” — Matthew 18:16, WEB
The language recalls Deuteronomy 19:15, where the testimony of two or three witnesses is connected to establishing a matter.
The principle is not that Christians should recruit supporters who will automatically agree with them.
It is that accusations and responses should be handled with care, corroboration, and fairness.
A witness is not supposed to be a cheerleader.
A witness is supposed to help establish the truth.
This is why a faithful church should not be satisfied with hearing only the most influential person's version of events.
It should not assume the wealthiest donor is innocent.
It should not assume the longest-serving volunteer is always right.
It should not assume the person who cries most convincingly is necessarily telling the whole story.
It should not assume the quieter person is lying.
And it should never mistake someone's spiritual vocabulary for evidence of spiritual integrity.
Truth must matter more than status.
Evidence must matter more than popularity.
And justice must matter more than preserving the appearance of peace.
Because a congregation can look peaceful while people inside it are being crushed.
It can sing about freedom while silencing those who need help.
It can preach about holiness while protecting unrepentant wrongdoing.
It can talk about grace while demanding that the wounded bear consequences the offender refuses to face.
That is not the beautiful unity Jesus prayed for.
That is a counterfeit peace purchased with someone else's suffering.
Then comes the sentence that many Christians would rather avoid.
“If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly.” — Matthew 18:17, WEB
In the Greek:
εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ
eipe tē ekklēsia
“Tell it to the church.”
The noun ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) refers to an assembly or congregation. In this context, it points to the community of believers.
This does not mean that every dispute should immediately become a public spectacle, a social-media post, or an announcement before a congregation.

The precise way a church responsibly involves its recognized leadership and, when necessary, its gathered membership will depend upon the nature of the matter and its biblical understanding of church governance.
But the central point is unmistakable.
When serious, established wrongdoing remains unresolved after appropriate efforts at correction, the matter cannot always remain a private dispute.
The community has responsibilities.
Not merely to the person who sinned.
Not merely to the person who was harmed.
But to the truth, to the holiness of the Church, and to the honor of Christ.
This is where the teaching becomes uncomfortable.
Because we live in a world that often treats correction as hatred.
Yet the Bible says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” — Proverbs 27:6, WEB
A friend who tells you the truth may hurt your pride.
But a friend who flatters you while you destroy your life is not helping you.
There are moments when love speaks gently.
There are moments when love listens patiently.
And there are moments when love must say:
“This cannot continue.”
Not because love has disappeared.
But because love refuses to cooperate with destruction.
Think of the person who has been hiding an addiction while telling everyone they are fine.
Think of the husband or wife whose secret dishonesty is tearing apart a family.
Think of the church member who continually manipulates others but calls every correction persecution.
Think of the believer who has been confronted repeatedly, not over a difference of opinion or a harmless mistake, but over genuine wrongdoing they refuse to abandon.
At some point, silence stops being kindness.
At some point, avoidance becomes participation.
At some point, the fear of offending someone begins to outweigh the fear of dishonoring God.
But there is a warning here for those who enjoy confronting others.
If the possibility of church discipline excites you because you finally have an opportunity to expose someone you dislike, examine your heart.
If you secretly hope the person refuses to repent because their downfall would satisfy you, examine your heart.
If you use biblical language to humiliate someone rather than pursue truth and godliness, examine your heart.
Galatians 6:1 says that those who are spiritual should restore someone caught in a trespass in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
The word translated “restore” comes from καταρτίζω (katartizō), a verb associated with putting something into proper condition or order.
Restoration is not casual approval of sin.
But neither is it the delight of watching another person collapse.
It is a sober, humble pursuit of what is right.
Because the person being corrected is not the only sinner in the room.
Every one of us stands in need of mercy.
Every one of us has blind spots.
Every one of us has said something we wish we could take back.
Every one of us has failed to love perfectly.
And if we forget that while confronting someone else, our own pride may become another sin demanding repentance.
Then Jesus says something even harder.
“And if he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.” — Matthew 18:17, WEB
Those words can sound devastating.
And they are serious.
Within the covenant community, persistent refusal to repent may eventually require the Church to stop treating someone as a member in good standing.
Other passages, including 1 Corinthians 5:1–13 and Titus 3:10–11, reinforce the reality that the Church must sometimes draw boundaries in response to grave and persistent wrongdoing.
But notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not command hatred.
He does not authorize cruelty.
He does not give believers permission to threaten, harass, mock, or dehumanize anyone.
And here is the detail that should make us stop.
How did Jesus treat tax collectors?
He called Matthew, a tax collector, to follow Him.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He entered the home of Zacchaeus, whose encounter with Jesus was accompanied by a transformed response to his wrongdoing.
Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
But He did not declare sinners beyond the reach of grace.
So when Matthew 18 describes treating an unrepentant person as a Gentile or tax collector, it must be understood alongside the rest of Scripture.
The person may no longer be affirmed as a faithful member of the believing community.
But that does not mean they cease to be a human being worthy of truthful witness, appropriate compassion, and a genuine call to repentance.
Church discipline is not a declaration that someone is beyond salvation.
It is a recognition that persistent, unrepentant conduct cannot simply be affirmed as Christian faithfulness.
And when repentance becomes evident, the Church must not become so attached to punishment that it forgets the possibility of restoration.
Second Corinthians 2:6–8 describes a situation in which Paul urges the believers to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward a person who had received sufficient correction.
Christians debate the precise relationship of that passage to the case in 1 Corinthians 5, but its instruction about reaffirming love is unmistakable.
Correction must never become an excuse for endless cruelty.
And restoration must never be reduced to a rushed declaration that everything is normal again.
Because repentance has fruit.
John the Baptist said:
“Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!” — Matthew 3:8, WEB
In Greek, the word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It speaks of a change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin toward God.
It is not merely embarrassment at being discovered.
It is not simply sadness over consequences.
It is not an emotional performance designed to regain trust without changing behavior.
True repentance involves acknowledging wrong, turning from it, and pursuing obedience.
Where harm has occurred, repentance may also require restitution, transparency, accountability, and acceptance of consequences.
Zacchaeus did not merely tell Jesus that he felt sorry.
He responded with concrete commitments to generosity and restitution in Luke 19:8.
And that distinction matters.
Because someone can cry during an apology and still refuse to change.
Someone can quote Scripture while continuing to manipulate others.
Someone can say, “God has forgiven me,” while refusing to take responsibility for the damage they caused.
God's forgiveness is not a license to evade accountability.
And the fact that a victim chooses to forgive does not automatically mean trust has been rebuilt.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness does not require pretending that the danger has ended.
Reconciliation requires truth, and restored trust ordinarily requires credible evidence of change over time.
A person may be forgiven and still face legal consequences.
A leader may repent and still be unqualified to return to leadership.
A relationship may be released from bitterness without becoming safe to resume.
That is not a failure of grace.
It is an acknowledgment that grace does not abolish wisdom.
Now consider the words that follow.
“Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven.” — Matthew 18:18, WEB
The Greek includes the expressions ἔσται δεδεμένα (estai dedemena) and ἔσται λελυμένα (estai lelymena).
These are future forms of “to be” combined with perfect passive participles, often understood as emphasizing a state already established.
The passage concerns the serious responsibility of the Church to make judgments consistent with God's revealed will.
It does not give a congregation the power to force heaven to approve whatever it decides.
A church cannot turn injustice into righteousness by voting for it.
A pastor cannot transform personal preference into divine law by declaring it from a pulpit.
A leadership team cannot call something holy merely because its members agree.
The Church is accountable to Christ.
Not the other way around.
And that should make every person exercising spiritual authority tremble with humility.
Because spiritual authority is never permission to become spiritually unaccountable.
Jesus continues with His teaching about agreement in prayer and then says:
“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.” — Matthew 18:20, WEB
Many Christians know that verse.
We quote it during small prayer meetings.
We use it when attendance is low.
We remind ourselves that Jesus is present even when only a few believers gather.
That encouragement is consistent with the broader truth of Christ's presence with His people.
But in Matthew 18, the immediate context is not simply the size of a prayer gathering.
It is the solemn responsibility of believers dealing with sin, truth, agreement, and accountability under Christ's authority.
“In my name” is not a magic phrase that makes every decision righteous.
It means gathering under the authority and character of Jesus.
And Jesus is never honored when His name is used to defend what His Word condemns.
This is why the Church must take these words seriously.
Not with arrogance.
Not with fear-driven secrecy.
But with reverence.
Because when believers gather to address serious wrongdoing, they are not playing with religious procedures.
They are handling matters that affect real lives.
Real marriages.
Real children.
Real friendships.
Real reputations.
Real spiritual wounds.
Real souls.
And all of it must be brought under the lordship of Christ.
But Matthew 18 does not end with the command to tell it to the Church.
Peter asks Jesus a question that exposes something painfully human.
“Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” — Matthew 18:21, WEB
You can almost hear the exhaustion.
How many times, Lord?
How many times do I have to face the pain of being wronged?
How many times must I wrestle with resentment?
How many times do I have to choose not to become consumed by what someone did?
Peter proposes seven times.
Jesus answers:
“I don't tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” — Matthew 18:22, WEB
The Greek expression is ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά (hebdomēkontakis hepta).
It is sometimes rendered “seventy-seven times” and sometimes “seventy times seven,” reflecting an expression also connected with Genesis 4:24.
The point is not a mathematical ceiling after which revenge becomes acceptable.
Jesus is confronting the human desire to place a convenient limit on forgiveness.
And then He tells the parable of the unforgiving servant.
A servant owes his king an enormous debt.
A debt beyond his ability to repay.
He begs for patience.
And the king responds with astonishing mercy.
The debt is forgiven.
But the same servant goes out and finds a fellow servant who owes him a far smaller amount.
Instead of showing mercy, he seizes him and demands payment.
When the fellow servant begs for patience, the forgiven servant refuses.
And suddenly, the story is no longer about someone else's hypocrisy.
It is about us.
How easily we forget the mercy we have received.
How quickly we demand grace for ourselves and strict judgment for everyone else.
How often we want God to remember our weakness while expecting Him to ignore the weakness of those who have offended us.
Yet this parable must not be twisted into telling abused people that they must remain in danger.
Jesus' command to forgive does not eliminate the need for justice, protection, or appropriate boundaries.
The parable confronts mercilessness and unforgiveness.
It does not require victims to deny reality or restore access to someone who remains unsafe.
And that distinction matters deeply.
Because the Gospel does not teach us to call darkness light.
It teaches us that Jesus Christ entered our darkness to rescue us from it.
Which brings us to the most important question in the entire passage.
Why would Jesus care so much about how His people handle sin?
Why insist on truth?
Why command correction?
Why make room for witnesses?
Why involve the Church when necessary?
Why teach forgiveness immediately afterward?
Because sin is not merely a social inconvenience.
It is rebellion against a holy God.
It damages human relationships.
It deceives the heart.
It hardens the conscience.
And ultimately, it separates sinners from the life they were created to enjoy in fellowship with God.
But Jesus did not come merely to expose sinners.
He came to save them.
And that is where Matthew 18 leads us beyond the difficult conversation, beyond the wounded relationship, beyond the congregation struggling to do what is right.
It leads us to the cross.
There, the sinless Son of God was condemned.
There, the innocent One suffered.
There, the One who never lied was surrounded by false testimony.
There, the One who never sinned bore the judgment our sins deserved.
There, human wickedness reached an appalling display of cruelty.
And there, God revealed the astonishing depth of His redeeming love.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — WEB
Not when we had repaired ourselves.
Not when we had become impressive enough to deserve mercy.
Not when we had finally learned how to hide our failures beneath religious respectability.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
The Gospel is not that sin does not matter.
The Gospel is that sin matters so much that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
First Peter 2:24 says that Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness.
Notice both parts.
He bore our sins.
And He calls us to live to righteousness.
Grace does not merely excuse the past.
Grace begins transforming the person.
That is why the theme of scandal and grace is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the heartbeat of redemption.
Consider Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
He failed at a moment when courage was desperately needed.
Yet the risen Christ restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of shepherding His sheep in John 21.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
And Christ's restoring mercy was real.
But Jesus did not restore Peter by declaring that his denial never happened.
He met him in the truth.
He confronted the wound.
And He called him forward.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners who turn to Him.
And maybe this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Perhaps you have been carrying a wound from someone in the Church.
You have wondered whether Jesus saw what happened.
You have struggled to pray because every time you close your eyes, you remember the person who hurt you.
You have questioned whether you were wrong for speaking up.
Hear this.
Jesus is not indifferent to injustice.
He is not impressed by religious appearances that conceal wickedness.
He does not command you to protect someone else's sin at the cost of your safety.
You can seek help.
You can tell the truth.
You can establish boundaries.
You can pursue justice.
And you can bring your pain to Christ without pretending that healing has already happened.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.” — WEB
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You are the person who needs to repent.
You have justified your words.
Minimized your actions.
Blamed the person you wounded.
Called correction an attack.
Called accountability persecution.
You have been more concerned about whether people still respect you than whether you have actually made things right.
And now, something inside you is trembling.
Because you know the truth.
Do not run from that conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess what you have done.
Stop defending what God is calling you to forsake.
Seek forgiveness from those you have harmed when doing so is appropriate and safe.
Make restitution where possible.
Accept accountability.
Do not demand immediate trust as the price of your apology.
And do not confuse the painful consequences of sin with the absence of God's mercy.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — WEB
There is hope for the repentant sinner.
Not because repentance earns salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
His blood cleanses from sin.
His resurrection declares His victory over death.
His grace calls us out of darkness and into a new life.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy would be to read Matthew 18, recognize your own sin, feel the conviction of the Holy Spirit, and then close this article determined to change nothing.
Please do not do that.
Do not let another day become another excuse.
Do not let pride rob you of the freedom that comes with walking in the light.
And do not let someone else's failure persuade you that Jesus Himself has failed you.
The Church belongs to Christ.
And where His people fall short, His Word still stands.
Where leaders fail, His lordship remains.
Where relationships fracture, His truth remains.
Where repentance is genuine, His mercy remains.
And where a wounded believer can barely whisper a prayer, His compassion remains.
Maybe tonight, the most spiritual thing you can do is not write another religious post.
Maybe it is to apologize.
Maybe it is to tell the truth you have been afraid to tell.
Maybe it is to ask for help.
Maybe it is to stop spreading a story you have not verified.
Maybe it is to confront a wrong with humility instead of bitterness.
Maybe it is to forgive without pretending that trust has already been restored.
Maybe it is to admit that you have been using church attendance as a substitute for surrender.
Or maybe, after years of feeling unwanted, you simply need to hear this:
The Savior who spoke about the wandering sheep has not forgotten the wounded.
And the Savior who commands repentance still receives sinners who come to Him.
That is why Matthew 18 is difficult.
It leaves no comfortable hiding place for pride.
It confronts the gossip.
It confronts the hypocrite.
It confronts the unrepentant.
It confronts the self-righteous.
It confronts the community that values its reputation above the truth.
And it confronts the temptation to withhold mercy after receiving so much of it ourselves.
But above all, it points us toward the heart of Jesus.
A Shepherd who seeks the wandering.
A Lord who loves righteousness.
A Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
A King who refuses to treat holiness as optional.
And a Redeemer whose grace is powerful enough to transform the people who come to Him in faith.
Not as a performance.
Not to impress anyone.
But as a simple expression of where you are in your walk with God.
You may discover that someone reading your words has been fighting a similar battle in silence.

And if you are willing, share what Matthew 18 has taught you about truth, forgiveness, accountability, or restoration. Your testimony may help another believer understand the Scriptures more faithfully.
There may be someone who needs the courage to repent.
Someone who needs to stop gossiping.
Someone who needs to understand that forgiveness does not require tolerating ongoing abuse.
Someone who has walked away from fellowship because they confused the failures of Christians with the character of Christ.
And someone who has never truly understood why the Gospel calls us to both holiness and mercy.

If a particular person comes to mind, consider tagging them only if doing so would encourage rather than embarrass or expose them. You can also send this privately with a simple message: “I thought this might encourage you.”
Sometimes a quiet act of love reaches a heart more deeply than a public announcement.
Save it as a reminder that truth and love are not enemies in the kingdom of God.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to join us.
Not because following a page makes someone more spiritual.
Not because a Facebook community can replace your local church.
But because daily exposure to Scripture, biblical teaching, prayerful encouragement, and Christ-centered discipleship can help us keep our attention on the Savior in a world filled with distraction.
There is room here for honest questions.
For biblical correction.
For testimonies of God's faithfulness.
For people learning to surrender.
For believers who have stumbled and are getting up again by the grace of God.
And for those who are discovering that following Christ is not about maintaining a flawless religious image.
It is about trusting the Savior who died and rose again and learning to obey Him.

Every article we write, every biblical teaching we prepare, every devotional resource we share, and every effort to reach people with the message of Jesus Christ requires time, commitment, and resources.
Our desire is to continue and expand this work so that more people can encounter Scripture faithfully explained, hear the call to repentance, and discover the hope of the Gospel.
Scripture teaches:
“Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, WEB
Salvation is not purchased by financial support.
And no one should feel pressured to give beyond their means.
There is something beautiful about believers choosing to support the spread of God's Word.
Not to earn grace.
But because they have received grace.
Not to purchase a blessing.
But because they desire to be a blessing.
Not because the Gospel is for sale.
But because proclaiming the Gospel faithfully is a mission worth supporting.
These products are not what makes our mission worthwhile.
Jesus Christ is.
You can benefit from them, share them, and encourage others to grow in God's Word.
We would be grateful to walk alongside you in this journey of Scripture, discipleship, conviction, healing, and spiritual growth.
But before you leave, I want to return to the words that began this entire conversation.
“Tell it to the church.”
Not because the Church is perfect.
Not because its leaders are incapable of making mistakes.
Not because every accusation is true.
Not because every conflict deserves public exposure.
And certainly not because anyone has the right to weaponize the Bible against the vulnerable.
But because Jesus calls His people to be a community where truth matters.
Where sin is taken seriously.
Where the wounded are not discarded.
Where the accused are treated fairly.
Where repentance is more than a performance.
Where correction is carried out with humility.
Where forgiveness is not confused with the removal of consequences.
And where restoration, when possible, is pursued for the glory of God.
The Church must never become a place where people are more afraid of telling the truth than they are of continuing in sin.
And it must never become a place where people are so eager to expose another person's failure that they forget their own desperate need for mercy.
We need both.
Truth that refuses to compromise.
And grace that refuses to abandon the repentant.
That is the difficult beauty of Matthew 18.
It calls us away from cowardly silence and cruel condemnation alike.
It calls us to follow Jesus.

And perhaps, when all the arguments have ended, when the emotions have settled, when the excuses have fallen apart, and when we finally stand before the Lord who knows every hidden thing, the question will not be whether we managed to protect our image.
It will be whether we trusted Him enough to walk in the light.
Because the cross of Jesus Christ is not where God pretended sin did not exist.
It is where the terrible seriousness of sin and the immeasurable mercy of God met in the sacrifice of our Savior.
And the empty tomb declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So if you need to repent, come to Christ.
If you need to seek help, do not remain silent.
If you need to make things right, begin walking in truth.
If you are weary, seek His strength.
If you have been wounded, remember that the failures of people do not erase the faithfulness of Jesus.
And if God has shown you mercy, let that mercy shape how you treat others.
The deepest scandal is not that Jesus knows the truth about us—it is that He knew it all, went to the cross for sinners, and still calls us to come into the light.
